conventions.rule: The battle is shown only as an image wrought by a god on a shield given to Aeneas, a prophecy of a future far beyond the story's time. Draft each step as what the poem depicts on the shield, and do not take its order or details as a historian's sequence unless the verse itself links them.
conventions.why: The account is a description of an artwork set inside a mythic narrative, not a narrative of the battle.

evidence.quotation: For the shield's central glory could be seen great fleets of brazen galleys, and the fight at Actium
the Lord of Fire had cunningly portrayed

conventions.rule: In the shield scene, Caesar, alone or with the title Augustus, means the young victor of the battle, the Augustus entity, not Julius Caesar. The title is given before he held it.
conventions.why: The person entity's aliases include Julius-style names that a reader might wrongly map to the dictator.

evidence.quotation: Caesar Augustus led Italia's sons to battle
But Caesar in his triple triumph passed the gates of Rome

conventions.rule: Cleopatra is never named. She appears as the Queen or as Antony's Egyptian wife, and you should map these to the Cleopatra entity only where the shield context makes it plain. Elsewhere in the poem, the Queen also denotes Dido or Juno, so decide from context.
conventions.why: The same epithet points to different women across the poem.

evidence.quotation: In the midst, the Queen, sounding her native timbrel
But what can cheat true love? The Queen foreknew his stratagem

conventions.rule: The poet writes as a partisan of the victor. Moral colouring such as barbarism, shame, monstrous foreign gods, or the blessing of the Roman gods is his rhetoric. Record it as an interpretation note rather than as fact about the fighting.
conventions.why: Value judgments are woven into the description.

evidence.quotation: Opposing, in barbaric splendor shine the arms of Antony
Her monster-gods, barking Anubis, and his mongrel crew

conventions.rule: Gods, personifications, and similes in the battle scene are poetic figures. Do not draft gods or abstractions as participants, and do not draft comparisons as events. For example, the flight of the eastern peoples is attributed to a god's bow; draft only the flight itself.
conventions.why: The scene mixes divine machinery and epic simile with the human action.

evidence.quotation: There Actian Apollo watched the war, and o'er it stretched his bow
like hills on hill-tops hurled, or Cyclades drifting

conventions.rule: Agrippa leads a squadron in a neighbouring position, but the verse does not say which wing. Do not assign him a specific wing from this source, and do not map the peak named Leucate to the Actium promontory entity.
conventions.why: The force entities are more specific than the poem supports, and the headland named is not among the place's aliases.

evidence.quotation: in neighboring region great Agrippa leads, by favor of fair winds and friendly Heaven, his squadron forth
Leucate's peak glowed o'er the golden tide

conventions.rule: Speeches, prayers, and laments put in characters' mouths are the poet's composition. Treat them as rhetoric, not as reports of what was said.
conventions.why: Much of the text is composed direct speech.

evidence.quotation: Then Drances rose, that foe inveterate

conventions.rule: The transcription has scanning errors: a capital I often stands for a lower-case l, letters are miscopied, and some proper names lack capitals. Read through these silently when identifying names.
conventions.why: Garbled spellings could mislead name matching.

evidence.quotation: from his Iofty seat the helmsman Palinurus
in beautiful array of Tyriao purple

notes: Only one sampled passage concerns the inquiry's event, the shield ekphrasis; the rest is mythic narrative of Aeneas. The triumph and temple-giving on the shield are later aftermath, not battle steps. The source gives no dates.
